title: Do Hangover Pills Actually Work? An Honest Look at the Evidence
excerpt: Do hangover pills work? An evidence-based look at DHM, Blowfish, ZBiotics, Myrkl, prickly pear, Korean hangover pills, and charcoal, and what actually helps.
metaDescription: Do hangover pills work? What the research says about DHM, Blowfish, ZBiotics, Myrkl, prickly pear, Korean pills and charcoal, ranked by evidence.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most hangover pills don't work as well as their packaging suggests, and none of them come close to the one thing that reliably works, which is drinking less. A few ingredients have small, early studies showing modest benefits for some symptoms. Others are built around a mechanism that sounds clever but has never been tested properly in people. And one popular category is really just an old-fashioned painkiller with a hangover label on the box. If you understand which is which, you can stop wasting money and make a sensible choice.

**The quick verdict:** Large reviews of the research have repeatedly found no strong evidence that any pill, supplement, or drug prevents or cures a hangover. That's not the same as saying everything is useless. Some ingredients (such as DHM, prickly pear extract, and a handful of plant extracts used in Korean hangover drinks) have small studies or animal research suggesting they might take the edge off. Painkiller-based products can genuinely ease a headache, but they come with real safety trade-offs when alcohol is involved. Activated charcoal and most "detox" blends have little to support them. Below, we sort the main categories by how strong the evidence actually is, and link to our full reviews for each product so you can dig deeper.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes published research and product labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Hangover supplements are sold as dietary supplements, which means the FDA does not review them for safety or effectiveness before they go on sale. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before trying a hangover product if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver, kidney, or stomach problems, take blood thinners, antidepressants, diabetes medicine, or any regular prescription, or have been told to avoid aspirin or NSAIDs. **Get medical help right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, or has blue-tinged or very pale skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no pill helps with that. In the US, call 911.

## Why Hangovers Are So Hard to Treat With a Pill

Before judging any product, it helps to know why this is a hard problem. A hangover isn't one thing going wrong. It's several things happening at once, and scientists still argue about which ones matter most.

The main suspects are:

- **Acetaldehyde.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, which is toxic. It's cleared fairly quickly in most people, and researchers disagree about how much it contributes to the hangover you feel the next morning, since symptoms often peak after blood alcohol has already dropped to zero.
- **Inflammation.** Research on hangovers has found changes in immune signaling molecules (called cytokines) after heavy drinking. This may explain the achy, flu-like feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Much of the next-day fog may simply be sleep loss.
- **Dehydration and stomach irritation.** Alcohol makes you urinate more and irritates the stomach lining. These contribute to thirst, headache, and nausea, though studies suggest dehydration alone doesn't explain how bad hangovers feel.
- **Congeners.** Darker drinks like bourbon and red wine contain more of these by-products of fermentation, and they appear to make hangovers worse for some people.
- **Low blood sugar and disrupted brain chemistry.** Alcohol affects the brain's GABA and glutamate systems, and the rebound as it wears off may add to the jittery, anxious feeling some people get.

Because there are so many moving parts, a pill that targets just one of them can only ever help with part of the picture. A product that claims to "fix" hangovers would need to address all of them, and nothing on the market has been shown to do that. You can read more about the underlying biology in our [complete hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025).

## What the Big Research Reviews Found

When scientists want to know if something works, the strongest evidence comes from systematic reviews, which gather every good-quality trial on a question and look at them together.

**A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ*** (by Pittler, Verster, and Ernst) looked at randomized trials of hangover treatments and concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary intervention was effective for preventing or treating hangovers.

**A 2022 systematic review in the journal *Addiction*** (led by researchers at King's College London) revisited the question with more recent trials. It found that a few substances, including clove extract, tolfenamic acid (an anti-inflammatory drug), pyritinol, Hovenia dulcis fruit extract, L-cysteine, red ginseng, and Korean pear juice, showed some improvement in individual studies. But the authors rated the quality of that evidence as very low. Most trials were small, many were run on young men, several were funded by manufacturers, and few results had been repeated by independent teams. Their conclusion was that no hangover remedy could be recommended with confidence.

That's the honest backdrop for every product below. When a brand says its formula is "clinically studied," it usually means one ingredient appeared in one small study, often at a different dose, sometimes in animals.

## The Main Types of Hangover Pills, Ranked by Evidence

Here's how the main categories stack up. "Evidence" here means published research in people, not marketing claims or customer reviews.

| Category | Examples | What it's supposed to do | Strength of evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Painkiller-based | Blowfish (aspirin + caffeine) | Ease headache and fatigue | Good for headache relief; real safety caveats with alcohol |
| DHM supplements | No Days Wasted, Double Wood, Flyby, Cheers | Support alcohol metabolism, reduce next-day symptoms | Promising animal research; limited human data |
| Prickly pear | Standalone or in blends | Reduce inflammation-related symptoms | One small human trial showed partial benefit |
| Korean and Japanese hangover products | Condition, Dawn 808, Ukon no Chikara | Plant extracts like Hovenia dulcis and turmeric | A few small studies; very low quality |
| Probiotic "pre-drink" products | ZBiotics, Myrkl | Break down alcohol or acetaldehyde in the gut | Plausible idea; mostly company-funded research |
| Vitamin and electrolyte blends | B-vitamin "morning after" packs | Replace nutrients, support hydration | Weak for hangovers specifically |
| Activated charcoal | Charcoal capsules | "Absorb" alcohol and toxins | Poor; charcoal binds alcohol badly |

Let's go through each one.

## Painkiller-Based Pills: They Work, But Know What You're Taking

The hangover pills with the most reliable short-term effect are the ones that contain an actual drug. [Blowfish](/never-hungover/blowfish-hangover-review), for example, is an over-the-counter product that combines aspirin with caffeine. That's essentially the same combination found in many standard headache tablets. Aspirin can ease a pounding head, and caffeine can blunt grogginess. So people often report feeling better, and that's not just placebo.

The catch is that you're taking an NSAID (a type of anti-inflammatory painkiller) on a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. The aspirin label in the US carries a warning about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day. Aspirin also thins the blood, so it isn't suitable for people on blood thinners, people with ulcers, or anyone told to avoid it. Caffeine can worsen dehydration slightly and make jitteriness or anxiety worse.

A few practical rules if you choose this route:

- Take it the morning after, with food and water, not before bed while alcohol is still in your system.
- Don't stack it with other painkillers that contain aspirin or ibuprofen.
- Remember that it treats symptoms. It does nothing for the underlying causes of the hangover.

If you're weighing up painkillers in general, our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explain the stomach and liver risks of each in plain terms. The short version for acetaminophen (Tylenol) is especially important: don't take it to "head off" a hangover, because alcohol and acetaminophen together can stress the liver.

## DHM Supplements: The Most Interesting Science, Still Early

DHM (dihydromyricetin) comes from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis), which has been used in traditional East Asian medicine for centuries. It's the main active ingredient in many Western hangover supplements, including No Days Wasted, Double Wood, Flyby, and Cheers Restore.

**Why researchers are interested.** The best-known study is a 2012 paper in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues at UCLA. In rats, DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on GABA receptors in the brain (the same system alcohol affects). Other lab and animal studies have suggested DHM may help the liver process alcohol and its by-products and may reduce markers of liver stress. A small 2015 randomized trial in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease reported improvements in some liver markers, which is encouraging for liver health but isn't a hangover study.

**What's missing.** There are very few well-designed human trials looking directly at DHM and hangover symptoms. Most of what you read on supplement websites extrapolates from rat studies. That doesn't mean DHM doesn't work. It means nobody has shown clearly how well it works in people, at what dose, or for whom.

**Our honest take.** DHM is the hangover ingredient with the most interesting mechanism and the most active research, and it's generally well tolerated in the studies that exist. It's a reasonable thing to try if you go in with realistic expectations. We've written a dedicated, evidence-only breakdown in [does DHM work? An honest science review](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025), and a summary of the human trials in [DHM randomized controlled trials](/never-hungover/dhm-randomized-controlled-trials).

For specific products, see our individual reviews of [Flyby Recovery](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025), [Cheers Restore](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review), [No Days Wasted](/never-hungover/no-days-wasted-dhm-review-analysis), and [Good Morning hangover pills](/never-hungover/good-morning-hangover-pills-review-2025). Rather than repeat them here, the main differences come down to how much DHM is in each serving, what else is in the blend, and price per night.

## Prickly Pear: One Real Trial, Partial Benefit

Prickly pear cactus extract (Opuntia ficus indica) is one of the few hangover ingredients tested in a randomized, placebo-controlled human trial. A 2004 study in the *Archives of Internal Medicine* (Wiese and colleagues) gave volunteers prickly pear extract or placebo before drinking. The extract group reported less nausea, dry mouth, and loss of appetite, and had lower levels of an inflammation marker called C-reactive protein. However, it didn't significantly improve several other symptoms, including headache, and overall hangover severity was only modestly reduced.

That's a mixed result, but it's more than most ingredients have. It also fits the idea that inflammation plays a role in how bad a hangover feels. Prickly pear shows up in several blends, sometimes at doses much lower than the study used. We compare it head to head with DHM in [DHM vs prickly pear for hangovers](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers).

## Korean and Japanese Hangover Products

Hangover drinks and pills are a huge market in South Korea and Japan. Popular products such as Condition and Dawn 808 use plant extracts, often including Hovenia dulcis (the same tree DHM comes from), while Japan's Ukon no Chikara is built around turmeric.

The research behind these is a mix of small human studies, many from Korea, plus animal work. Some, such as studies on Hovenia fruit extract and Korean pear juice, made it into the 2022 *Addiction* review mentioned above, which found some positive results but rated the evidence very low quality. The products are popular, inexpensive, and generally considered low risk for healthy adults, but popularity isn't proof. Our full breakdown of the brands, ingredients, and what each study actually measured is in [Korean and Japanese hangover pills](/never-hungover/korean-japanese-hangover-pills).

## Probiotic Pills: ZBiotics and Myrkl

A newer category takes a different approach: using bacteria to break down alcohol or its by-products in your gut before they reach your bloodstream.

- **ZBiotics** is a genetically engineered probiotic designed to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde in the gut. The idea is clever, but most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, not the gut, and the main evidence comes from the company rather than independent trials. We cover this in detail in our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review).
- **[Myrkl](/never-hungover/myrkl-review)** uses a strain of Bacillus subtilis plus vitamins, and is marketed as breaking down alcohol in the gut. A small company-backed study reported lower blood alcohol levels in people who took it before drinking. That is a different question from whether people feel better the next morning, and it hasn't been widely repeated by independent researchers.

There's also a practical concern worth stating plainly. A pill that lowers your blood alcohol might lead some people to drink more, thinking they're protected. It won't make it safe to drive, and it doesn't change your legal limit.

User sentiment on both is split. On forums like Reddit, some people are enthusiastic and others say they noticed no difference and found the price hard to justify. That pattern, strong fans plus many who shrug, is what you'd expect from a product with a small real effect, a large placebo effect, or both.

## Vitamins, Electrolytes, and "Morning After" Blends

Many hangover products are mainly B vitamins, vitamin C, magnesium, zinc, and electrolytes. The logic is that drinking depletes nutrients and fluids, so topping them up should help.

There's some truth to the hydration part. Alcohol does make you urinate more, and replacing fluids helps with thirst and some headaches. But you can get most of that from water, a sports drink, or an oral rehydration solution. A few small studies have looked at B vitamins and zinc in relation to hangovers, mostly based on diet questionnaires rather than controlled trials, and the results are too weak to rely on. For a healthy person who isn't deficient, a vitamin pill after one night out is unlikely to make a noticeable difference.

If you want to get the hydration piece right, our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing. The same logic applies to stick-on products, which we examine in [do hangover patches work?](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work).

## Activated Charcoal: One of the Weakest Options

Activated charcoal is used in hospitals for certain kinds of poisoning because it can bind some substances in the gut. That's where the hangover idea comes from. The problem is that charcoal binds alcohol very poorly, and alcohol is absorbed into the bloodstream quickly, largely from the stomach and upper small intestine. Studies in people have found that charcoal doesn't meaningfully lower blood alcohol.

Charcoal can also bind to medications and nutrients, so it can reduce the effect of other pills you take around the same time, and it can cause constipation. It's one of the weakest options in this whole category. We explain the details in [does activated charcoal help a hangover?](/never-hungover/activated-charcoal-hangover).

## Why So Many People Swear Their Pill Works

If the evidence is this thin, why do hangover pills have thousands of glowing reviews? A few reasons, and none of them mean the reviewers are lying.

1. **The placebo effect is strong for subjective symptoms.** Headache, fatigue, and "feeling rough" are exactly the kind of symptoms that respond to expectation. Believing you've taken something that helps can genuinely make you feel better.
2. **People change their behavior when they take a pill.** Someone who remembers to take a supplement before bed often also drinks water, eats something, or stops drinking a bit earlier. Those habits help, and the pill gets the credit.
3. **Hangovers vary a lot from night to night.** The same number of drinks can leave you fine one morning and wrecked the next, depending on sleep, food, what you drank, and how fast. Without a controlled comparison, it's easy to credit a good morning to whatever you took.
4. **Unhappy customers are less likely to write reviews,** and many hangover brands offer refunds or perks that encourage positive ones.

None of this proves a given product doesn't work. It explains why customer reviews can't tell you whether it does. That's why we lean on controlled trials in our [supplement reviews](/reviews), and say clearly when they don't exist.

## How to Judge a Hangover Pill Before You Buy

You don't need a science degree to spot the better products. Ask these questions:

- **Does the label list exact amounts of each ingredient?** "Proprietary blends" that hide doses make it impossible to compare a product with the research.
- **Is the main ingredient at a dose close to what was studied?** A sprinkle of prickly pear or DHM is unlikely to do what a full study dose did.
- **Is there third-party testing?** Supplements aren't checked by the FDA before sale, and independent testing for purity and contamination is a meaningful sign of quality.
- **Does it make claims that sound too good?** Words like "cure," "eliminate," or "drink without consequences" are red flags. Honest brands say "support" and stop there.
- **What's hiding in the formula?** Check for aspirin, acetaminophen, or caffeine, which can interact with alcohol, other medicines, and health conditions.
- **Is it safe with your medications?** Ask a pharmacist. It takes five minutes and can prevent real problems. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers common questions.

## What Actually Works Better Than Any Pill

Every review of the evidence lands in the same place: the only reliable way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. After that, the habits with the most support are simple and cheap.

- **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies. Drinking faster than that lets alcohol build up.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream.
- **Alternate with water.** It slows your drinking and helps with fluid loss.
- **Choose clearer drinks.** Vodka and gin tend to contain fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy, or red wine.
- **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each of these in more detail. If you're already hungover, [ginger](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) has reasonable evidence for nausea in general, and food, fluids, and rest do most of the work.

## Who Should Skip Hangover Pills Entirely

Some people should avoid hangover products, or at least check with a doctor first:

- People who are **pregnant or breastfeeding**
- People with **liver or kidney disease**, or stomach ulcers
- Anyone taking **blood thinners, antidepressants, sedatives, seizure medicines, or diabetes medicines**
- Anyone with an **aspirin or NSAID allergy** (relevant for painkiller-based products)
- Anyone under the legal drinking age

And one more point that matters. If you find yourself relying on hangover pills most weekends, or you regularly feel shaky, anxious, or unwell the morning after unless you drink again, that's worth a conversation with your doctor. Those can be signs that your body is reacting to alcohol in a way a supplement can't fix.

## If You Want to Try DHM

If you've read all this and still want to try a hangover supplement, DHM is the one we think has the most interesting research behind it, as long as you treat it as a possible helper rather than a guarantee. Take it with water, follow the label dose, and keep doing the basics above. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when.

Two options we've reviewed: [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple, low-cost, single-ingredient choice, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a pricier blend that adds L-cysteine, milk thistle, and other ingredients. Neither replaces drinking less, and neither makes it safe to drive or to combine alcohol with medicines you've been told to avoid.

## The Bottom Line

- No hangover pill has strong evidence that it prevents or cures hangovers. Major research reviews in 2005 and 2022 both reached that conclusion.
- Painkiller-based pills like Blowfish do ease headaches, but aspirin and alcohol together can irritate the stomach, and they're not for everyone.
- DHM has the most interesting science, mostly from animal studies, with limited human data. Prickly pear has one small human trial with partial benefit.
- Probiotic products like ZBiotics and Myrkl rest on clever ideas but mostly company-funded research.
- Activated charcoal and most vitamin blends have little to support them for hangovers.
- Drinking less, eating, pacing yourself, and drinking water remain more effective than anything in a bottle.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do hangover pills actually work?**

Mostly not as well as advertised. Systematic reviews of the research published in 2005 and 2022 found no strong evidence that any pill or supplement prevents or cures hangovers. A few ingredients, including DHM, prickly pear, and some plant extracts used in Korean products, have small or early studies suggesting modest benefits for certain symptoms. Painkiller-based products can ease a headache. None of them replace drinking less.

**What is the most effective hangover pill?**

There's no clear winner, because no product has strong head-to-head trial evidence. For headache relief specifically, painkiller-based products like aspirin-and-caffeine pills tend to work, but they carry stomach risks after drinking. Among supplements, DHM has the most active research and a plausible mechanism, though human data are limited. Prickly pear has one small trial showing partial benefit.

**Are hangover pills safe?**

Most hangover supplements are generally well tolerated by healthy adults, but they aren't reviewed by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale. Products that contain aspirin, acetaminophen, or caffeine have real interactions with alcohol and some health conditions. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if you're pregnant, have liver, kidney, or stomach problems, or take any regular medication.

**Should you take hangover pills before or after drinking?**

It depends on the product. Supplements like DHM, prickly pear, and probiotic products are usually labeled for before or during drinking. Painkiller-based products are meant for the morning after, with food and water. Never take acetaminophen (Tylenol) before or while drinking to prevent a hangover, because the combination can stress the liver.

**Does Blowfish work for hangovers?**

Blowfish combines aspirin and caffeine, so it can genuinely ease a hangover headache and grogginess, much like a standard headache tablet with coffee. It doesn't address the underlying causes of a hangover. Because aspirin can irritate the stomach and raise bleeding risk, especially after drinking, it isn't suitable for people with ulcers, those on blood thinners, or anyone told to avoid aspirin.

**Does activated charcoal prevent hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Activated charcoal binds alcohol poorly, and alcohol is absorbed into the bloodstream quickly. Studies in people found that charcoal doesn't meaningfully lower blood alcohol. It can also interfere with medications taken around the same time.

**Why do so many people say hangover pills work for them?**

Hangover symptoms are subjective and vary a lot from night to night, so the placebo effect is strong. People who remember to take a pill also tend to drink water, eat, or stop earlier, and the pill gets the credit. That doesn't mean every product is useless. It means customer reviews can't tell you whether a product works, which is why controlled trials matter.
